svg.title: Why summarization in a hub-and-spoke link-state network lets a branch become transit, and the three fixes
svg.desc: Left side is the topology: Spoke-A connects to Hub-1, Hub-1 to Hub-2 over the core, Hub-2 to Spoke-B, and a backup circuit exists between Spoke-A and Spoke-B. Right side is the failure chain in four steps: Hub-1 summarizes spoke routes into the Spoke-A area, Spoke-A now has only the summary and sends everything to Hub-1, Hub-1 computes that reaching Spoke-B via Spoke-A is cheaper because the backup link is in the topology, and traffic bounces between Spoke-A and Hub-1 until it dies. Below, three fixes: make the spoke stub or totally stub so it holds only a default route, keep an unsummarized link between the ABRs so detail is exchanged at the boundary, or filter the summaries the spoke should not receive. A closing note says the spoke must be a pure leaf.
svg.text: A summary that is correct for the core can make a branch become transit
The loop is not a protocol bug: SPF only sees cost, and the summary removed the detail it needed
TOPOLOGY
Hub-1
ABR, summarizes spokes
Hub-2
ABR, core side
core link
Spoke-A
area 10, summary only
Spoke-B
area 20
backup circuit that SPF can see
The backup link is the trap. It is legitimate redundancy for data,
but it is also an edge inside the area topology — so Hub-1
computes “to reach Spoke-B, go through Spoke-A”.
Spoke-A cannot disagree: after summarization it holds only
10.20.0.0/16 via Hub-1, so it sends everything back.
THE FAILURE CHAIN
1. Hub-1 summarizes all spoke /24s into 10.20.0.0/16 and advertises it into area 10.
Spoke-A's table shrinks from 800 routes to 1. The project is declared a success.
2. Spoke-A wants Spoke-B: only the summary matches, next hop Hub-1.
Correct so far — Hub-1 forwards onward and the packet arrives.
3. Hub-1 runs SPF: Spoke-B is reachable via Spoke-A over the backup circuit,
and that cost is lower than the core path. The detail it needs was never advertised.
4. Hub-1 hands the packet back to Spoke-A. Spoke-A has one route: to Hub-1.
The packet bounces until TTL expires. Every engineer blames the protocol.
WHY THE SUMMARY CAUSED IT
Summarization removed the detail that would have told Hub-1
“Spoke-A is not on the path to Spoke-B”. Spoke-A's own table is now
too coarse to break the tie, so both ends believe the other is closer.
THREE FIXES — PICK ONE PER SITE, NOT ONE PER NETWORK
Fix 1 — make the spoke a pure leaf: stub or totally stub, so it holds a default route and takes no transit decision at all.
Fix 2 — keep an unsummarized link between the ABRs: detail crosses the boundary where it is needed, and nowhere else.
Fix 3 — filter what the spoke receives: a distribute-list that drops summaries the site should never have had.
The practical rule: when hub-and-spoke runs a link-state protocol, the spoke must be a pure leaf — exactly one egress route and no transit decision.
Any design that lets a spoke “choose a path” buys you suboptimal routing, and eventually buys you a loop.
